newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Malaysia seeks to expand non-edible palm uses.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia seeks to expand non-edible palm uses.

text.p: Malaysia aims to increase the oleochemical uses of its palm oil, an industry symposium heard on Wednesday.
"Malaysia can become the world's oleochemical centre," Salmiah Ahmad of the semi-governmental research body PORIM told the Lipidex 97 oilseeds conference and trade fair.
"There is enough supply, enough processing capacity, adequate infrastructure and government support."

She said domestic oils products -- both in food uses such as cooking and in non-food applications such as detergents, printing ink or cosmetics -- were acceptable to all groups. Some excluded competing tallow in food and non-food uses because of its animal origin.
Malaysia's oleochemical production capacity in 1995 was at one million tonnes, exceeding government plans to achieve 807,000 tonnes by that date, when world oleochemicals capacity was 5.26 million.
The total capacity of the ASEAN region was 1.64 million tonnes, and multinational companies were assisting the region in developing the industry, she said.
Malaysia aimed to raise oleochemical capacity to 1.2 million tonnes by 2000.
Oleochemicals include fatty acids, fatty methyl esters, fatty nitrogen compounds and glycerine, derived in Malaysia from palm oil, palm kernel oil and their refined products such as stearin.
Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand were also offering coconut oil as a local raw material while industrialised countries needed to rely on imported raw materials for many oleochemical products.
Oleochemical uses were still dwarfed by food uses both at home and abroad.
The Malaysian industry received just 10.1 percent, or 892,000 tonnes, of total domestic palm oil and palm kernel oil production in 1995.
